1: A 7-second PyTorch job from a user whose finished jobs usually run about 14 hours (median 10^4.7 s). It is a new script (no finished runs in its group), so the model leans on the user's history, as the baseline does. A 7-second success is plausibly a job that exited at once (for example on a wrong argument) yet still ended as Terminated; the trace cannot confirm why, and nothing in the request distinguishes it from a real training run.
2: The same pattern as case 1 from the same user minutes later (39 submissions in the past hour). Repeated near-identical misses are why we bootstrap by user: one user's burst is not 39 independent pieces of evidence.
3: A TensorFlow job that ran 2.9 days. The user's past jobs were short (median 70 s) and failed 87% of the time, and the script group had never finished. The model's range tops out at about 3 hours. The truth lies outside the range, so a long successful run here was a genuine surprise given everything known at submission.
4: From the heaviest user (247,690 finished jobs). Its script group's 3 earlier runs took about 18 s, so the model trusted the group and predicted 30 s; this run took 17 hours. The user-level baseline (35 min) was closer by accident of averaging. Group history is usually the most informative feature, but it can mislead, probably when the same script is run on very different data (the trace does not show inputs).
5: A typical miss: predicted 7.6 min, actual 5 min (a factor of 1.5). The user's history and the script group agree, and the range (1.5 min to 1.8 h) contains the truth.
6: Another typical case: a frequent user (27,297 finished jobs) and a well-known script group (52 runs). Predicted 1.6 h, actual 1.1 h; both the model and the baseline are close and the range is narrow (40 min to 3.8 h).
7: A user with no finished history. Model and baseline both fall back to cluster-wide behaviour (about 13 min) and the job took 51 s. The model's range is much wider for such jobs (13 s to 12 h), which is the honest answer when nothing is known.
8: One of the rare jobs that request a specific GPU type (16 × V100M32). Large explicit requests from this user usually ran for about 19 hours, but this run took 72 s. The user's failure rate is 89%, so short runs that still end as Terminated are plausible. With so few explicit-type jobs the model cannot learn much about them; on test it is worse than the baseline for P100, T4 and V100M32 requests.
9: The model lost to the baseline here. The user submitted 768 jobs in the previous hour, a burst, and the model predicted 3 min. The job ran 21 hours, closer to the script group's usual 4.3 hours. We checked whether bursts simply mean short jobs: in development, successful burst jobs (over 500 submissions per hour) actually ran slightly longer than average (median 21 vs 11 min), though 77% of burst jobs failed. So this is an unexplained interaction rather than a simple rule. Trees can learn combinations that do not hold in a new period.
10: The model gave a 99.98% failure risk and the job succeeded. The user's past failure rate was 82% during a burst (47 submissions in the last hour), the pattern that dominates band 2. In development, 77% of jobs submitted in large bursts failed. Calibrated risk is still not certainty: some jobs in a failing burst succeed.
11: A missed failure. The user (1% past failure rate) and the script group (1,102 runs, none failed) both looked very safe, so the model gave 0.3%. A failure caused by something outside the request (a node fault or a changed input) cannot be predicted from the submission.
12: A user with no history. The model gave 53% risk against a 20% fallback, because the request pattern (a 1-GPU TensorFlow job submitted during the band-2 surge) resembles failing jobs. It did fail. Without history the model still ranks better than a constant guess, but with much less confidence.
